extracted.intended_audience: physicists/mathematicians and experimentalists studying fluid resistance, pendulum experiments, and classical mechanics
extracted.subtask_description: Designing, analyzing, and interpreting experiments and propositions to determine the resistance of bodies (especially spheres) moving in fluids, and related results about efflux and fluid pressure; includes how to extract quantitative resistance laws from pendulum-decay data and vessel-efflux analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efflux velocity equals velocity from falling through head (Torricelli-type law)
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole motion of the water effluent is that which the weight of the water perpendicularly incumbent on the orifice could generate; the velocity with which water issues from an orifice equals the velocity a body would acquire by falling through the height of the water above the orifice (expressed in the page as: 'motus aquæ totius effluentis is erit quem pondus aquæ foramini perpendiculariter incumbentis generare possit').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantitative relations are given relating orifice area A, head height (altitudo) A/2S etc., and reference falling distance S in time T; assumptions require a very fluid ('fluido subtilissimo') so that the simple relation holds. When applying, use the head (vertical depth) to compute efflux speed; correct for non-ideal fluids (viscosity, orifice narrowness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Volumetric flow proportional to orifice amplitude (area)
rubrics_metrics.description: The quantity of water flowing out in a given time is proportional to the amplitude (area) of the orifice through which it flows ('quantitas aquæ dato tempore defluentis erit ut amplitudo foraminis per quod defluit').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This proportionality is asserted under the hypothesis of an ideal/subtle fluid; for thicker fluids or narrow orifices the observed flow will be reduced. Use area scaling when converting efflux velocity to volumetric discharge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oblique efflux trajectories are parabolic (projectile shape)
rubrics_metrics.description: When water issues obliquely through a channel, in non-resisting spaces it describes a parabola whose parameter (latus rectum) is the height of the water in the vessel above the channel's orifice ('describet ... Parabolam cujus latus rectum est altitudo aquæ in vase supra canalis orificium').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply projectile motion kinematics (neglecting resistance) with the vertical head determining the parabola's parameter; for real fluids include viscous losses and narrower orifices which reduce range.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real fluids and narrow orifices reduce efflux relative to ideal prediction
rubrics_metrics.description: If the fluid consists of thicker particles, the efflux will be slower than the ideal relation indicates, especially if the orifice is narrow ('Nam si aqua ex partibus crassioribus constet, hæc tardius effluet ... præsertim si foramen angustum sit').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat Torricelli-style calculations as upper-bound/ideal; adjust experimentally (or via viscosity corrections) for real fluids and small orifices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pressure distribution: vessel supports weight except at orifice; removing pressure by efflux generates motion
rubrics_metrics.description: A filled vessel with an orifice sustains the weight of the whole water except the weight of the part perpendicular to the orifice; when the orifice is opened the pressure previously borne by the obstacle is removed and that weight produces efflux ('vas sustinebit pondus aquæ totius, dempto pondere partis illius quod foramini perpendiculariter imminet ... & pondus quod obstaculum sustinebat ... faciet ut aqua descendat & per foramen defluat').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hydrostatic reasoning to relate pressure support and resulting efflux-driving weight; account for how opening lateral outlets changes support and pressure distribution on vessel walls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resistance on a sphere equals the weight of a column of fluid whose base equals the gap area and height equals RS (action of fluid on sphere)
rubrics_metrics.description: The contrary action of the water on the sphere (resistance) equals the force that would generate the same motion — i.e., equals the weight of the column of water whose base equals the area between the sphere and the canal and whose altitude is RS ('actio contraria aquæ in Globum æqualis est vi ... ponderi columnæ aquæ, quæ Globo perpendiculariter imminet & cujus altitudo est RS').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When modeling the resistance of a sphere in a channel or fluid, identify the effective column of fluid displaced/impeded and equate its weight to the resisting force; this is used to convert impeded-volume arguments into force expressions under the ideal-fluid hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantity of fluid impeded by a sphere scales with square of diameters (gap/basis area)
rubrics_metrics.description: The quantity of water whose descent the sphere impedes is to the quantity that would descend if the sphere were removed as the base of the cylinder about the sphere is to the orifice — equivalently as the square of the sphere's diameter to the square of the cavity's diameter ('quantitas aquæ ... ut quadratum diametri Globi ad quadratum diametri cavitatis canalis').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cross-sectional-area (diameter squared) scaling when comparing impeded flows for differently sized spheres or cavities; this underpins the area-proportional flow and area-proportional resistance arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action and reaction: sphere and fluid forces balance (Newton's third law applied to fluid interactions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The action of the sphere on the descending water and the reaction of the water on the sphere are equal and opposite; the fluid's action on the sphere equals the force that would either remove or produce the same motion ('Actio & reactio aquæ per motus Legem tertiam æquantur inter se').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use equal-and-opposite force reasoning when converting impeded-fluid weight into the resisting force on solids; ensures momentum/impulse bookkeeping in efflux and sphere-in-fluid problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: A moving fluid whose parts are at rest relative to each other carries along floating bodies of equal density
rubrics_metrics.description: Any fluid progressing with accelerated motion, whose parts remain at rest relative to each other, carries along all floating bodies of the same density and transports them with the same velocity ('Fluidum omne quod motu accelerato ... rapit omnia ejusdem densitatis innatantia corpora, & secum cum eadem velocitate defert').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an entrainment criterion: if the fluid has cohesive internal motion (parts move together), solids of equal density will be entrained; useful when reasoning about flows carrying suspended bodies or frozen inclusions in experiments or thought experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resistance of spheres approximately scales with square of diameter (area) in the limit of fine fluid particles
rubrics_metrics.description: The resistance of a solid sphere, when the size of the solid increases indefinitely (or when the fluid is subdivided to arbitrarily small particles), is given approximately by the quantity of fluid displaced, i.e., scales roughly as the square of the semidiameter (cross-sectional area) ('resistentia solidi ... ut spatium Cylindricum per quod solidum movetur, adeoque in duplicata ratione semidiametri solidi quamproxime').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use area-based scaling (diameter^2) to predict how resistance changes with sphere size for sufficiently large spheres and very fluid media; experimental corrections (boundary layers, thread drag) can adjust the observed scaling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resistance does not diminish indefinitely by subdividing fluid; a lower limit exists
rubrics_metrics.description: One cannot suppose that the resistance to projectiles decreases indefinitely by infinite subdivision of the fluid; after a certain degree of fluid thinness (e.g., air, water, mercury), further subdivision will not much reduce the resistance ('postquam competentem Fluiditatis gradum acquisiverit ... resistentia in anteriore superficie solidi, per ulteriorem partium divisionem non multum minuetur').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When modeling or extrapolating resistance to ever-finer fluids, assume a limiting resistance; do not assume arbitrarily small resistance from theoretical subdivisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental method: deduce resistance law by measuring pendulum oscillation decay and fitting velocity-dependent terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure the loss of motion (difference between first descent arc and final ascent arc) over many oscillations for spheres suspended as pendulums; fit the observed arc-differences as a polynomial in V (e.g., A V + B V^{3/2} + C V^2) to determine coefficients that describe resistance components (linear, intermediate power, quadratic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform multiple experiments with different maximum speeds (different initial arcs) to create independent equations for A, B, C. Use chords/arc measurements to relate to V and solve the linear system for coefficients. Apply corrections for non-ideal geometry (cycloid vs circle) as discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate resistance components (linear, V^{3/2}, quadratic) empirically
rubrics_metrics.description: The observed resistance can be decomposed into additive parts: proportional to V (first power), to V^{3/2}, and to V^2; coefficients A, B, C are found from experimental data ('differentia arcuum sit AV + BV^{3/2} + CV^2' and subsequent fitting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use experiments at multiple velocities to determine each coefficient; compare experiments in different media to isolate terms (e.g., comparing air and water to isolate the V^2 term).

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental controls and corrections: account for thread resistance, vessel geometry, and boundary effects
rubrics_metrics.description: When conducting pendulum-decay experiments, correct for the resistance of the suspension thread (which can be significant), avoid small/close vessel boundaries which impede flow, and use sufficiently large vessels and appropriately spaced test bodies to minimize confinement effects ('resistentia fili ... de pendulorum inventa resistentia subduci debet' and notes on vessel size and Arca narrowness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate and subtract thread drag from total measured resistance; ensure the container (arca) is large relative to the pendulum sphere so that water flow is not artificially impeded; where necessary use compound pendulums or submerged configurations to reduce boundary artifacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare media (air vs water) to isolate resistance terms and infer density-proportional components
rubrics_metrics.description: By measuring identical pendulum experiments in two media (air and water) and comparing oscillation counts and arc-differences, one can deduce ratios of total resistances and isolate the portion proportional to the square of velocity — which scales roughly with fluid density ('resistentia penduli in aqua est ad ejus resistentiam in aere ut 535 ad 123/110' in the example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use matched experimental setups and account for differing oscillation periods; scale velocities appropriately when comparing results between media to extract density-proportional resistance components.

rubrics_metrics.name: If fluid-particle reflections are fully elastic, impulses double; intermediate reflection yields intermediate resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: If fluid particles are reflected from the body with maximum elastic effect, their impulses on the body are doubled; then the resistance of a spherical body would be half that in the other construction; if reflection is intermediate, resistance takes an intermediate value ('si particulæ Fluidi per vim suam Elasticam quam maxime a Globo reflectantur ... manifestum est quod ... resistentia ... duplo minor ... Si particularum vis reflexiva neque maxima sit neque omnino nulla, sed mediocrem aliquam rationem teneat: resistentia pariter ... mediocrem rationem tenebit').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When hypothesizing collision/interaction models between fluid particles and bodies, account for the reflection coefficient; entirely elastic vs entirely inelastic particle reflections change the computed resistance significantly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use geometric progression of sphere sizes and multiple repeats to extrapolate asymptotic behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform experiments with spheres whose diameters are in geometric progression (e.g., 4,8,16,32 digits) and use the progression of results to infer how resistance behaves for still larger spheres and to approach limiting theoretical relations ('Si Globi sumantur in proportione Geometrica ... colligetur quid in Globis adhuc majoribus evenire debeat').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments with sizes spaced geometrically to reveal scaling laws cleanly; combine multiple repeats and sizes to reduce noise and estimate asymptotic scaling.
